abstract: Cortical layering, fascicle geometry and tissue texture of the mouse brain lie in the mesoscopic range. That range sits below the hundred-micrometre sampling of a whole-brain magnetic resonance (MR) volume and above the micrometre structure of individual fibre bundles. Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) reaches into it, and MRI does not. Super-resolution models can enlarge an MR volume to any grid, but the grid size does not decide what the volume contains. We take PS-OCT at 10 um isotropic sampling as the target and ask whether a 100 um MRI volume still carries information about each target band. At each candidate magnification we ask whether the source still determines something about the target band. Two readouts on a shared band index answer it. The bands come from an isotropic spherical-shell decomposition. The energy readout predicts a log-RMS energy envelope, which needs no unobservable phase, and a structural-tensor comparison separates geometric from intensity guidance, with the absolute cosine read against an analytic level of 0.50. On nine paired mouse brains the two readouts do not weaken together. The median absolute cosine falls from 0.864 at 1x to 0.661 at 4x and to 0.518 at 10x, while the R-squared of the energy envelope decays from 0.627 to 0.438 at 4x and to 0.175 at 10x. The two readouts part company at 4x, a target voxel of 25 um, the last of the six candidates at which both conditions hold. Each candidate interrogates a different physical scale. The curves therefore cannot carry a claim about a special frequency, and we report the boundary as the output of a procedure and not as a constant. Two further effects pull the readouts in opposite ways. One is intrinsic to the envelope kernel and accounts for part of the accelerated decay beyond 4x. The other comes from the smoothing applied to the reference before it is scored.
